thresholds.label: 18 °C: salmon swim less well; BC guideline (weekly mean of daily max) for streams

source.title: DFO Fraser River Environmental Watch report, 14 Sep 2026 (temperature effects on migrating sockeye)

value.note: DFO Fraser River Environmental Watch (2026): "18°C - Decreased swimming performance". The BC Water Quality Guideline for temperature (2001) sets MWMT (mean weekly maximum temperature) = 18 °C for streams where fish distribution is unknown, and Chinook migration's optimum range tops out at 19.0 °C (Table 2).

satellite.reason: The gauges publish water temperature, which beats any satellite value here: the lower Salmon River is roughly 10-30 m wide, narrower than a Landsat thermal pixel (100 m, resampled to 30 m) or an ECOSTRESS pixel (70 m), so a river-pixel 'surface temperature' would mostly measure the warm banks and hay fields in summer.

species.evidence: BC 2026 release: "more than 200 adult Chinook salmon in the watershed" by 19 Aug 2026; BC work windows list Chinook arriving after the late-July window.

sources.title: BC Government news release 2026WLRS0042-000965 (Salmon River temporary protection order)
BC Ministry of Environment, Salmon Arm Forest District instream work windows (2005)

species.evidence: Counting-fence report: "the chinook run peaks between Sept. 10 and 15"; over by early November.

sources.title: Salmon Arm Observer, "Chinook numbers down" (6 Nov 2015; counting-fence results)

species.stage: eggs in gravel, then juveniles rear one year in fresh water
species.evidence: COSEWIC 2020: DU13 spawns in Shuswap tributaries "such as the Seymour, Eagle, Scotch and the Salmon rivers"; "the juveniles in DU13 stay in freshwater for one year"; "more vulnerable ... to water management issues (esp. Salmon River)". Status: Endangered (2020).

sources.title: COSEWIC assessment and status report, Chinook Salmon (2020): DU13 South Thompson Stream Summer 1.3

species.evidence: Early Nov 2015: "the coho salmon run is just getting started on the Salmon River". Spawning months for this river were not in a source we could open.

sources.title: Salmon Arm Observer, "Chinook numbers down" (6 Nov 2015; counting-fence results)

species.evidence: BC work windows list coho (CO) in the Salmon River; coho juveniles rear a year in fresh water (general life history).

sources.title: BC Ministry of Environment, Salmon Arm Forest District instream work windows (2005)

species.evidence: BC work windows list sockeye (SK) in the Salmon River, but we found no public source giving Salmon River sockeye months. Shuswap-system sockeye generally spawn in early autumn (DFO Fraser sockeye); we leave the strip empty rather than guess.

sources.title: BC Ministry of Environment, Salmon Arm Forest District instream work windows (2005)

run_timing.irrigation_note: Months where the engine's current rotation (alfalfa hay) needs at least 5 mm of irrigation on average (2015-2025 weather): the overlay for the strip.

critical_window.why: Lowest flows of the year, warmest water, and adult Chinook entering and spawning: the same weeks the hay field's irrigation need is still high. The orders (16 Aug 2023; 19 Aug 2026) fall here.

run_timing.note: Months are from Salmon River sources where we found them; anything Shuswap- or Fraser-general is labelled. Check local timing with the Secwépemc Fisheries Commission or DFO before acting on it.

water_for_salmon.note: One 21.5 ha field is a small share of the river; the orders exist because hundreds of licences add up, in the weeks when the river is lowest. A rotation with no Aug-Sep irrigation (dryland sainfoin-grass) leaves that water in the river.

summary: In August 2026 the Salmon River near Salmon Arm averaged 0.33 m³/s, 29% of a normal August, and spent 54 days of Aug-Sep below the 0.625 m³/s level in the 2026 protection order.
August 2023 averaged 0.74 m³/s; the 2023 order's level was 1.27 m³/s.

Water temperature at the gauge reached 24.7 °C in summer 2026, with 56 days that reached 18 °C (salmon swim less well) and 51 that reached 20 °C (high pre-spawn mortality risk) between June and September.
Adult Chinook enter in August and spawn in September, the same weeks hay fields still want water.

This field's current hay rotation would draw about 23,642 m³ in Aug-Sep (4.5 L/s, about 0.7% of a low August flow). Small alone; hundreds of licences together can match the whole river. The dryland sainfoin-grass rotation draws none.

Early hint (rule of thumb, not a forecast): of the indicators with 20+ years, winter precipitation in the valley lines up best with August flow (rank correlation 0.45 over 34 years; 6 of its 12 driest-third years had a low August).
